nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  White Shrimp
Scientific Name:  Penaeus setiferus

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Kingdom: Animalia
	Phylum: Arthropoda
	Class: Malacostraca
	Order: Decapoda
	Family: Penaeidae

Note: 	Subphylum: Crustacea

Other Common Names:  Blue shrimp, blue-tailed shrimp; Common shrimp; Daytona shrimp; Gray shrimp; Green shrimp, green-tailed shrimp; Lake shrimp; Rainbow shrimp; Southern shrimp (495 496).

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Linnaeus)
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  White shrimp were the only species fished for in the shrimp fishery until the mid-1930's; other species were darker and therefore undesirable.  The species is fished for throughout the nearshore Gulf of Mexico and along the Atlantic coast.  The offshore fishery has averaged 4.8 and 16.3 million pounds heads off from 1960-1982 for Texas and Louisiana, respectively (384).  White shrimp are used as a bait fishery throughout the bays and nearshore waters using otter trawls from June to October.

Recreational:  Approximately 8.8 and 5.2 million pounds (heads on) of total shrimp were taken by recreational shrimpers in 1979 and 1980, respectively, in Texas and Louisiana (250).

Ecological Role:  White shrimp are preyed on by many of the endemic finfish.  The postlarvae and juveniles are more tolerant of lower salinity water than other Penaeus species (767 785) and may venture further into brackish marshes.  White shrimp may be displaced by brown shrimp from Spartina marshes to nearby mud substrates (233 787).

Jackson (353) found mercury to be two orders of magnitude more toxic than zinc for juvenile white shrimp with higher mortalities occurring at higher temperatures.  Mortalities were also higher during spring compared to winter.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  White shrimp range from Fire Island, NY, to the St. Lucie Inlet, Florida on the Atlantic coast.  In the Gulf of Mexico, from Ochlocknee River, Florida, to Campeche, Mexico; they are rarely found near the dry Tortugas, Florida.  Centers of abundance occur off Georgia and northeastern Florida for the Atlantic coast; and Louisiana, Texas and Tabasco for the Gulf of Mexico (767).  SAB (681) reports the range from Apalachee Bay, Florida to northeast Campeche Bay, Mexico.  Perez-Farfante (545) distinguishes the area of Ciudad, Mexico as the southern limit in the Gulf of Mexico.

Within Study Area:  Postlarval to subadult white shrimp are well established throughout the Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi estuaries and nearshore Gulf waters, utilizing the nursery habitat generally from June/July through October/November.

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
Eggs: are demersal.
Larval: stages are planktonic.  Postlarvae become benthic upon reaching the nursery areas of estuaries seeking habitats of shallow water, with muddy/sand bottoms high in organic detritus, or abundant in marsh grass in moderate to low salinities.  As shrimp grow they leave the marsh habitat for deeper parts of the estuary prior to their emigration to Gulf waters (411).
Adults: generally inhabit nearshore waters of the Gulf in depths less than 27 m, and usually more abundant at a depth of 14 m (589).  White shrimp have a life expectancy of 18 months, although some have been maintained in the laboratory for 3-4 years (385).

White shrimp postlarvae immigrate to the estuarine nurseries through passes from May to November, with peaks in June and a second peak in September for the northwest Gulf of Mexico (385 37).  Juveniles migrate farther up the estuary into less saline water than brown or pink shrimp (545).  Emigration of juvenile and subadult white shrimp is related to sharp drops in water temperature occurring from October to December (576).  There is a predominate westward movement of white shrimp in offshore waters (425).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  Neritic to estuarine, pelagic to demersal, depending on life stage.  Juveniles prefer shallow, marsh or muddy sand bottoms in estuarine bays.

Substrate:  Postlarvae and juveniles inhabit mostly muddy or peaty bottoms with large quantities of decaying organic matter.  Adults are found on bottoms of soft mud or silt in offshore waters.  (545 767).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity:  White shrimp can be considered euryhaline since most of their life stages can tolerate wide ranges of salinities.
Postlarvae: have been collected in salinities ranging from 0.4 to 37.4 ppt.
Juvenile: prefer salinities less than 10 ppt (785).
Adults: are usually found offshore in waters with salinities greater than 27 ppt (496).

Temperature:  White shrimp are more tolerable of high temperatures and less tolerable of low temperatures than brown or pink shrimp (118).
Postlarval: white shrimp have been collected in temperatures from 12.6-30.6 C.
 Juveniles: have been collected in temperatures ranging from 6.5-39.0 C, with peaks in abundance between 15 and 33 C (785).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Sexual reproduction with external fertilization (496).

Mating/Spawning: Spawning for the Atlantic coast is probably begins in May and extends through September (412 767); in the Gulf the season probably extends from March to September or October (spring to late fall) (223).  Spawning is offshore 9-34 m deep and peaks in the summer (June-July).  Females that spawn early may spawn a second time in late summer or fall.  Rapid temperature changes, such as the sudden increases and decreases that occur in the summer and fall, seem to trigger spawning (298).

Fecundity: A large female is estimated to produce 0.5 to 1.0 million eggs at a single spawning (12 767).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Ripe eggs are 0.2 to 0.3 mm in diameter and hatch in 10 to 12 h after fertilization (385).

Larvae and Juvenile: Larvae transform through 5 naupliar stages, 3 protozoeal stages and 3 mysis stages.  The larval life stages are 10 to 12 days long, dependent on local food and habitat.  They enter the estuaries as postlarvae at lengths of 7 mm TL (411). There is little or no growth below temperatures of 18 C (785).  Juveniles have attained lengths of 98-146 mm TL in 4 to 6 weeks (785).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: White shrimp are omnivorous at all feeding stages.  Foods consist of detritus, parts of annelids and gastropods, fish parts and bryozoans, sponges, corals, filamentous algae, and vascular plant stems and roots (118).
